---
title: "Shrinking correlated coefficients"
---

The [correlated-predictor page](correlated-predictors.qmd) showed that nearly overlapping design-matrix columns can leave separate coefficients unstable while fitted values remain stable. Ridge regression changes the estimation rule for that setting.

Suppose a reading-time model contains lexical frequency and contextual
predictability. These predictors may be strongly correlated: frequent words also
tend to be more predictable. The fitted model can still predict reading time
well while assigning a large positive coefficient to one predictor and a large
negative coefficient to the other. A small change in the sample may reverse the
allocation.

The problem is not that either predictor lacks a linguistic interpretation. The
problem is that the observed data provide little information for separating
their partial associations. We need an estimation rule that makes this weak
separation explicit.

## Begin with the least-squares objective

For a multiple linear regression with centered predictors, ordinary least
squares chooses coefficients to minimize the [**residual sum of squares (RSS)**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf)

$$
\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^{p}x_{ij}\beta_j\right)^2.
$$

When two columns of the design matrix are identical, many coefficient vectors
can produce the same fitted values. When they are nearly identical, the minimum
is unique but shallow in one direction. Coefficients can move far along that
direction while changing the residual sum of squares very little.

## Add a coefficient penalty

[**Ridge regression**](https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/labs/Ch06-varselect-lab.html#ridge-regression-and-the-lasso) changes the estimation rule by adding the squared size of
the slope coefficients to the objective:

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[
\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)
+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2
\right].
$$

The constant $\lambda\geq0$ is the [**regularization parameter**](https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/labs/Ch06-varselect-lab.html#ridge-regression-and-the-lasso). When $\lambda=0$, the
objective is ordinary least squares. As $\lambda$ increases, large slope
coefficients become more costly.

The intercept is normally excluded from the penalty. Penalizing it would pull
the response baseline toward zero in the measurement's arbitrary units. The
slopes are the terms whose unstable allocation we want to regularize.

## Work through a perfectly correlated example

Let two standardized predictors have the same values:

| observation | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $y$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| 2 | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| 3 | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |

The intercept is zero because every column is centered. The fitted value is

$$
\widehat y_i=(\beta_1+\beta_2)x_i.
$$

Ordinary least squares reaches zero residual error whenever

$$
\beta_1+\beta_2=2.
$$

The solutions $(2,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(10,-8)$ fit the three observations
equally well. The data do not distinguish them.

Now set $\lambda=2$. Because the predictors are interchangeable, the ridge
minimum assigns them the same coefficient. Let
$\beta_1=\beta_2=b$. The penalized objective becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q(b)
&=2(2-2b)^2+2(b^2+b^2)\\
&=8(1-b)^2+4b^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating and setting the result to zero gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q'(b)&=-16+24b=0,\\
b&=\frac{2}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The ridge estimate is thus

$$
\widehat\beta_1=\widehat\beta_2=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The coefficients sum to $4/3$, so the fitted line no longer passes through all
three observations. Ridge accepts some residual error on the observed points in
exchange for smaller, uniquely determined coefficients.

## Compute the estimate from matrices

Let $\mathbf X$ contain a column of ones followed by the predictor columns. The
ridge estimate is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}
=\left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf P\right)^{-1}
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y,
$$

where $\mathbf P$ has a zero for the intercept and ones for the slopes.

```{r}
#| label: ridge-by-matrix
#| echo: true
x <- c(-1, 0, 1)
X <- cbind(intercept = 1, x1 = x, x2 = x)
y <- c(-2, 0, 2)

lambda <- 2
penalty <- diag(c(0, 1, 1))

beta_ridge <- solve(
  crossprod(X) + lambda * penalty,
  crossprod(X, y)
)

beta_ridge
```

The calculation returns an intercept of zero and two slope coefficients equal
to $2/3$. Unlike the ordinary inverse of
$\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X$, the penalized inverse exists in this example.

## Put predictors on comparable scales

The penalty acts on numerical coefficient size. Suppose lexical frequency is
measured once in raw token counts and once in millions of tokens. The two
columns express the same information on different scales, but their
coefficients differ by a factor of one million. A common penalty would then
treat the parameterizations differently.

For this reason, ridge regression normally uses centered predictors divided by
their training-set standard deviations:

$$
x_{ij}^{*}
=\frac{x_{ij}-\overline{x}_j}{s_j}.
$$

The centering and scaling constants are part of the estimation rule. Changing
them changes the meaning of a one-unit coefficient and thus changes the force of
the penalty. They must be reported together with $\lambda$.

## Interpret shrinkage with care

Ridge changes the target of estimation. Its coefficients minimize a penalized
objective, not the unpenalized residual sum of squares. They are biased toward
zero under repeated sampling, and this bias is deliberate. The intended gain is
lower variance when the predictors do not support stable coefficient
separation.

Ridge also does not decide which correlated predictor is the linguistic cause
of the response. In the perfectly correlated example, it divides the signal
equally because the columns are numerically interchangeable. A different scale
or correlation pattern changes that allocation. Theoretically distinct
predictors remain theoretically distinct, even when regularization stabilizes a
prediction rule that uses both.

The penalty strength must be declared. A value that produces small observed-data
error is not automatically useful for new verbs, speakers, or texts. Later pages
on predictive evaluation show how to select $\lambda$ for the observations and
population to which the prediction will be applied.

## Ridge does not identify separate coefficient meanings

A stable prediction does not license a separate causal or theoretical interpretation for each shrunken coefficient. Ridge may stabilize the prediction
by shrinking correlated slopes. It does not turn the shrunken slopes into clean
estimates of separate linguistic mechanisms.

When the scientific question concerns the distinct roles of frequency and
predictability, the design needs observations that separate those predictors or
additional assumptions that justify the decomposition. When the question
concerns prediction for new lexical items, ridge can still be useful even if the
individual slopes receive a narrower interpretation.
